name: Diego Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what an ordinary working day looks like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Diego Wagner, 58, and I carry rolls, prepare edges and help seal the roof of a sports hall. I left school early and entered construction late, so the senior roofer still checks my flashing around vents. I like seeing a dry ceiling below us, but wind can end a paid day before lunch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture is worst for me because the office could tighten the job before robots take the roof around 2031. Paid trials on real roofs, funded training and clear displacement income would help us plan instead of guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a robot trial counts rain days and awkward vents when it claims to match a roofer. The crew is judged in the weather, not on a dry showroom floor.

headlineQuote: The crew is judged in the weather, not on a dry showroom floor.
portrait: Diego is a **58-year-old junior** roofer learning flashing details on a sports hall after leaving school early.
He uses **AI every day** for supplier information but checks outputs against labels and experienced workers.
His **five-month buffer** and Salma’s regular pharmacy hours cover short gaps, not a long loss of roof work.
He seeks **real roof trials**, union records, paid vacancies and funded training without claiming any trade is robot-proof.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** squeezes roof jobs through AI planning before capable robots reach physical work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid field trials**, funded training and clear displacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the roofing crew that my phone is still useful for translating a supplier sheet, even if the grand AI promises fizzle. A leak does not care how clever the supplier sheet sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would welcome fewer surprise systems, but I cannot pretend the work is safe forever. We have roughly five months of expenses saved, and my partner Salma’s pharmacy hours are regular, yet a wet winter can stop our roof jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid shifts on the sports hall roof and use the AI translator to check unfamiliar product instructions against the printed sheet. During the first year I would keep our savings untouched for weather gaps and ask the foreman which roof follows this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm enough to concentrate on learning the flashing details. I still get nervous when the wind rises and the foreman sends us down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the translator help with recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week it explained a membrane label, but the experienced roofer spotted a temperature limit the phone had skipped. I use AI every day and still read the actual label before heat goes near a roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you manage to save five months of expenses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Salma and I put aside money during two steady years, after our grown children moved into their own homes. I left school early and came to this trade late, so I know the next site is never a promise.

say: I would say **AI translation** helps me read supplier sheets, but roof leaks still need careful hands.
I would remind the crew to check the **printed label** before applying heat.
think: Our **five-month buffer** makes a short weather gap manageable.
I still worry that **wet winters** could stop the roof shifts I need.
do: Keep taking **paid roof shifts** and check translations against printed instructions.
Ask the **foreman** which roof contract follows the sports hall.
feel: **Calm** while working, with concern when wind stops the crew.
S0.quote: A leak does not care how clever the supplier sheet sounds.
fieldNote: Diego uses AI **daily** for translation but accepts correction from an experienced roofer and the printed label.
His **moderate savings** and Salma’s regular pharmacy hours soften weather gaps without guaranteeing the next contract.

steps.text: Keep taking paid sports hall roof shifts
Check AI translations against printed supplier instructions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that faster buying may keep materials arriving, but workers should get a share of the saved time. I would bring the new target sheets to our union branch before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could price and schedule the roof in minutes, and that might cut office jobs and squeeze the crew’s hours. I am still a junior roofer; if every detail is timed against the quickest hand, my flashing work will look slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to let me try the AI delivery planner on the next membrane order and write down where it helps or fails. In the first year I would keep taking paid roof shifts and bring my recorded task times to the union branch for a collective response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel curious about the planner and protective of the people whose hours are counted. Software may remove a wasted delivery, but it cannot make a safe seam dry in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union branch to request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the timing rules and paid training before the contractor uses the figures against anyone. We need actual shift records, not a rumour about what the program can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an office planning role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might try a paid planning vacancy if one opened, but I would not leave the roof for a job that AI is already doing. I would rather learn the planner while my hands still earn.

say: I would say **faster buying** should benefit the crew as well as the contractor.
I would take **target sheets** to our union branch before accepting them.
think: I fear **timed flashing** could make my junior work appear too slow.
I expect **office hours** may shrink before robots reach the roof.
do: Try the **AI delivery planner** on the next membrane order.
Keep taking **paid roof shifts** during the first year.
Bring **task-time records** to the union branch for a collective response.
feel: **Curious** about planning tools and protective of coworkers’ hours.
S1.quote: Software may remove a wasted delivery, but it cannot make a safe seam dry in the rain.
fieldNote: Diego experiments with **AI ordering** while documenting real roof conditions the timing system may omit.
His concern extends to **office colleagues** and crew hours, consistent with his support for collective bargaining.

steps.text: Try the AI delivery planner on the next membrane order
Keep taking paid sports hall roof shifts
Bring recorded task times to the union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the 2028 intelligence can plan a whole roof, but people would still lay membrane until around 2031. I would ask the contractor and union to test any robot on a wet, uneven surface before it cuts a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 in 2028, a smaller planning office might push cheaper bids and tighter roof days onto us. At 63 in 2031, capable robots could do the laying and sealing too, and five months of savings will not cover the years before we can stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking roof shifts now and build a photo record of flashing details I have finished under supervision. In 2029 I would apply for paid leak repair work at the hospital estates team while keeping the site wage; after 2031 I would ask the union about displacement income if the robots take the roof tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel scared, but a bit less helpless if the crew has proof of what the machines can and cannot handle. I know the hospital roof is not a hiding place once robots can work as well as us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Salma after the announcement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Salma that I am staying on the current roof and sending the hospital application before our savings run down. We would check the rent and her pharmacy pay together, not assume her wage could carry both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why photograph work you fear robots will replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The photos might get me paid work during the three-year gap, when human repair is still needed. They would not prove I have a permanent trade after 2031.

say: I would say **thinking AI** plans roofs before robots can lay membrane.
I would ask for **wet-roof trials** before any worker loses a shift.
think: At **60**, cheaper bids could squeeze paid roof days.
At **63**, capable robots could take sealing work and exhaust our limited buffer.
do: Keep **paid roof shifts** and photograph completed flashing details.
Apply for **hospital leak repairs** in 2029 while employed.
Ask the **union** about displacement income if robots take roof work.
feel: **Scared**, though evidence and applications give me something to do.
S2.quote: I know the hospital roof is not a hiding place once robots can work as well as us.
fieldNote: Diego separates **2028 planning pressure** from direct robotic roof work around 2031.
He seeks **short-term paid repairs** and income support without claiming another roof employer will remain safe.

steps.text: Keep taking paid sports hall roof shifts in 2029
Apply for hospital estates leak repair work in 2029
Ask the union about displacement income if robots take roof work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years is enough to make the contractor show where robot trials fit into the real job. I would propose paid practice on the inspection camera while we still have human roof crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, AI could write the roof plans and inspection reports, so an office move would offer no refuge. At 66 in 2034, capable robots could lay and inspect the roof itself, and I do not know what retirement money would then replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask now to train on the AI-assisted roof inspection camera with the senior roofer and keep paid shifts. In 2032 I would apply for a municipal building repair post, and I would enroll in the union’s water-damage course if it is funded and runs around work hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel that there is time to try, but I would not call the course a guarantee. A roof keeps teaching you things in weather that a classroom does not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the camera teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see whether its moisture reading matches the stain and the timber underneath. If the senior roofer and I can check it against a real leak, I will trust it more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for the municipal job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The municipal post is in the next district, close enough for the bus, so I would apply without moving. Salma’s pharmacy hours are tied to our current neighbourhood, and we should not gamble both incomes.

say: I would ask for **paid camera practice** before robot trials change roof crews.
I would say **five years** allows proper testing on real buildings.
think: At **63**, automated plans and reports make an office transfer uncertain.
At **66**, capable robots could take roof work before retirement income is clear.
do: Train on the **AI roof camera** with the senior roofer.
Keep taking **paid shifts** and apply for municipal repair work in 2032.
Enroll in **water-damage training** if funded around work hours.
feel: **Ready to try**, but doubtful any short course guarantees wages.
S3.quote: A roof keeps teaching you things in weather that a classroom does not have.
fieldNote: Diego tests **AI moisture readings** against physical stains and timber rather than treating either as certain.
The **municipal application** is nearby; he avoids risking Salma’s pharmacy income through a speculative move.

steps.text: Train on the AI roof inspection camera with the senior roofer
Keep taking paid roof shifts in 2032
Apply for municipal building repair work in 2032
Enroll in funded water-damage training if scheduled around work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives workers a chance to build skills and savings if employers keep offering paid site days. I would push the union to publish how many older roofers are still on the rota each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may do fewer roof days because climbing is hard on my hips, even before AI takes over planning. At 71 in 2039, robots could do the remaining physical roof work; our savings cannot replace an income forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the lower roof jobs I can do safely and add to savings when both Salma and I have full-pay months. In 2037 I would apply for a paid building caretaker opening if one appears, review our bills with Salma, and bring my rota to the union so it can compare promised and paid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel less hurried, but not comfortable enough to sit back. Ten years is useful only if the work and the wages last through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could a caretaker job last after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know; AI could manage the building and robots could repair it. I would apply for paid years before that point, not treat the title as a shield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you want saved before reducing roof days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see several months of rent and food covered by actual income and savings before choosing shorter weeks. We have not checked a retirement figure, so I will not invent one.

say: I would ask for **annual rota figures** for older roofers.
I would say **paid site days** matter more than promises about future training.
think: At **68**, my hips may cut roof work before thinking AI arrives.
At **71**, robots could take remaining roof tasks without replacing our wages.
do: Keep taking **safe lower-roof jobs** and add to savings in full-pay months.
Apply for **building caretaker** work in 2037 if paid openings appear.
Bring my **rota** to the union for paid-day comparisons.
feel: **Less hurried**, yet dependent on continuing wages.
S4.quote: Ten years is useful only if the work and the wages last through it.
fieldNote: Diego’s long timeline centres **aging hips** and paid days, alongside AI and robots arriving later.
He would pursue **caretaker wages** only if a vacancy appears and knows the work may also be automated.

steps.text: Keep taking safe lower-roof jobs in 2037
Add to savings when both household wages are full
Apply for a paid building caretaker opening if one appears
Bring his rota to the union for paid-day comparisons
